items.prompt: What is 'container orchestration'?
choices: A system that keeps a fleet of containers running as intended across multiple machines, without manual intervention
A tool for building container images
A single container that manages logging for other containers
A naming convention for containers running the same app
items.explanation: Orchestration is specifically about keeping many containers running correctly across many machines, handling placement and failure recovery automatically.
items.reference:
Container orchestration
🖥️ Many containers, many machines
🤖 No manual intervention needed
Why: it's what turns 'someone has to notice and fix it' into an automatic process.

items.prompt: In L1's scenario, what was actually missing from the team's manual two-server setup?
choices: Something constantly checking whether what's running matches what should be running, and acting without a human
A third server, which would have automatically fixed the problem
A faster on-call engineer
Nothing — the setup was already correct for their scale
items.explanation: L1 frames the gap as the absence of continuous, automatic checking and correction — not simply a capacity or staffing problem.
items.reference:
Container orchestration
🖥️ Many containers, many machines
🤖 No manual intervention needed
Why: it's what turns 'someone has to notice and fix it' into an automatic process.

items.prompt: What does 'desired state / reconciliation loop' mean?
choices: A declared target is continuously compared against actual observed state, and any gap triggers a corrective action
A one-time setup step run only when the cluster is first created
A manual checklist an engineer follows during an incident
A backup system that restores from a snapshot once a day
items.explanation: The reconciliation loop is defined by its continuous compare-and-correct behavior — it doesn't run once, and it doesn't wait for a human trigger.
items.reference:
Reconciliation loop
🎯 Desired state vs actual state
🔁 Continuous, not one-time
Why: this is the core mechanism that makes self-healing possible at all.

items.prompt: According to L1, what triggers a corrective action in the reconciliation loop?
choices: A gap between desired state and actual observed state
A scheduled maintenance window
A human explicitly requesting a health check
The cluster reaching a fixed uptime milestone
items.explanation: The loop reacts specifically to a detected gap between what was declared and what's actually running — not to a schedule or manual trigger.
items.reference:
Reconciliation loop
🎯 Desired state vs actual state
🔁 Continuous, not one-time
Why: this is the core mechanism that makes self-healing possible at all.

items.prompt: What does the 'scheduler' component decide?
choices: Which machine a given container should run on, based on available capacity and resource requirements
How often the reconciliation loop should run
Which container image version to deploy
When a human should be paged
items.explanation: The scheduler's job is specifically the placement decision — where a container goes, given capacity and requirements.
items.reference:
Node, pod, scheduler
🖥️ Node = a machine
📦 Pod = smallest schedulable unit
🧭 Scheduler = decides placement
Why: placement decisions are what turn 'a container needs to exist' into 'it's actually running somewhere.'

items.prompt: What is a 'pod', as defined in L1?
choices: The smallest schedulable unit — one or more containers always placed on the same node together
A single physical machine in the cluster
A backup copy of a container's data
A group of unrelated containers spread across different nodes
items.explanation: A pod groups one or more containers that are always scheduled together onto the same node — it's the unit the scheduler actually places.
items.reference:
Node, pod, scheduler
🖥️ Node = a machine
📦 Pod = smallest schedulable unit
🧭 Scheduler = decides placement
Why: placement decisions are what turn 'a container needs to exist' into 'it's actually running somewhere.'

items.prompt: What does 'self-healing' mean in this context?
choices: The reconciliation loop noticing lost containers after a node failure and rescheduling them, without a human paging in
A container automatically fixing bugs in its own code
A backup node that's always kept as an exact live mirror of another
An alert that pages an engineer faster than before
items.explanation: Self-healing is the practical outcome of the reconciliation loop — automatic detection and correction of a node failure's effects, with no human in the loop.
items.reference:
Self-healing
💥 Node dies → containers lost
🔁 Loop notices, reschedules
Why: it's the reconciliation loop's practical payoff, not a separate mechanism.

items.prompt: In L1's scenario, why didn't the app recover on its own at 3am?
choices: Nothing was watching the containers or comparing actual state to desired state — recovery required a human to notice
The surviving server had a hardware fault too
The team hadn't written any code for their app yet
The containers were configured to never restart under any circumstances
items.explanation: L1 is explicit that nothing was watching — there was no automatic comparison between desired and actual state, so nothing triggered without a human.
items.reference:
Self-healing
💥 Node dies → containers lost
🔁 Loop notices, reschedules
Why: it's the reconciliation loop's practical payoff, not a separate mechanism.

items.prompt: How many servers were running containers in L1's manual-ops scenario?
items.explanation: The team ran their containers by hand across 2 servers, one of which crashed at 3am.
items.reference:
The scenario
🖥️ 2 servers, manual containers
💥 One crashes at 3am
Why: a concrete failure grounds the abstract 'what's missing' question.

items.prompt: What time did the server crash in L1's scenario?
choices: 3am
Noon
During a scheduled deploy
L1 doesn't specify a time
items.explanation: The crash happens at 3am, when nobody is watching — which is exactly the situation an automated reconciliation loop is meant to handle.
items.reference:
The scenario
🖥️ 2 servers, manual containers
💥 One crashes at 3am
Why: a concrete failure grounds the abstract 'what's missing' question.

items.prompt: In L1's scenario, what finally fixes the outage?
choices: A paged engineer logs in and manually starts replacement containers
The dead server automatically reboots and restores everything
The app's containers restart themselves after a timeout
Nothing — the outage described in L1 is never resolved
items.explanation: L1 states the fix requires a human: a paged engineer logging in and manually starting replacements — exactly the manual step orchestration is meant to remove.
items.reference:
The scenario
🖥️ 2 servers, manual containers
💥 One crashes at 3am
Why: a concrete failure grounds the abstract 'what's missing' question.

items.prompt: According to L2's flowchart, what happens on most iterations of the reconciliation loop?
choices: No gap is found, and the loop does nothing
A container is always rescheduled every iteration
The loop pages an engineer as a routine check
The loop stops running once the cluster is stable
items.explanation: L2 notes explicitly that most iterations find no gap and take no action — the loop only reacts when actual state diverges from desired state.
items.reference:
The reconciliation flowchart
Compare desired vs actual
Match → do nothing; Gap → reschedule
Why: most cycles are boring by design — action only happens when something's actually wrong.

items.prompt: According to L2, how quickly does the reconciliation loop react after a node dies, compared to a human-paged process?
choices: Within seconds, at the next comparison — not whenever a human happens to be paged and awake
Only after the next scheduled maintenance window
It reacts at exactly the same speed as a human-paged process
It never reacts automatically — a human still has to trigger it
items.explanation: L2 contrasts the loop's near-immediate reaction (next comparison cycle) with the unpredictable delay of waiting for a human to notice and respond.
items.reference:
The reconciliation flowchart
Compare desired vs actual
Match → do nothing; Gap → reschedule
Why: most cycles are boring by design — action only happens when something's actually wrong.

items.prompt: According to L2, what's the downside of a scheduler that always packs the fullest node first?
choices: A single node failure can take out a disproportionate share of the fleet packed onto it
It always leaves every node completely empty
It's slower to compute than spreading
It requires more nodes than spreading does
items.explanation: L2 explains that packing concentrates containers onto fewer nodes, which means one node's failure has an outsized impact compared to spreading.
items.reference:
Spread vs. pack
📦 Pack: fills one node first
↔️ Spread: favors most free capacity
Why: spreading reduces how much one node's failure can take down.

items.prompt: According to L2, what trade-off does a spreading scheduler make compared to a packing one?
choices: It trades some packing efficiency for reduced blast radius on node failure
It has no trade-off — spreading is strictly better in every way
It trades node failure resilience for lower CPU usage
It only works with exactly 2 nodes
items.explanation: L2 states the trade-off directly: spreading is less packing-efficient but gains the resilience property that makes self-healing practical.
items.reference:
Spread vs. pack
📦 Pack: fills one node first
↔️ Spread: favors most free capacity
Why: spreading reduces how much one node's failure can take down.

items.prompt: According to L2's comparison table, what happens when there's no spare capacity anywhere and a node fails, under an orchestrator?
choices: The reconciliation loop reports the gap as unresolved (pending), rather than silently failing
The orchestrator automatically provisions new hardware to compensate
The orchestrator crashes entirely
The gap is silently ignored and never reported
items.explanation: L2's table is explicit: without spare capacity, the loop still runs and still reports the gap — it just can't close it, and it says so via pending status rather than failing silently.
items.reference:
Manual ops vs. orchestrator
🙋 Manual: a human decides everything
🤖 Orchestrator: automatic, but bounded by real capacity
Why: automation changes who notices and acts — it doesn't manufacture resources that don't exist.

items.prompt: According to L2's table, what changes about 'deciding where replacements go' between manual ops and an orchestrator?
choices: The scheduler evaluates every node's remaining capacity automatically, instead of a human picking a server by hand
Nothing changes — both approaches require the same manual server selection
The orchestrator picks servers at random regardless of capacity
Only manual ops can consider node capacity at all
items.explanation: L2's table contrasts manual server-picking (hopefully checking capacity by hand) against the scheduler's automatic evaluation of every node's remaining capacity.
items.reference:
Manual ops vs. orchestrator
🙋 Manual: a human decides everything
🤖 Orchestrator: automatic, but bounded by real capacity
Why: automation changes who notices and acts — it doesn't manufacture resources that don't exist.

items.prompt: According to L2's closing point, why does headroom (deliberately unused capacity) need to be planned for?
choices: Because the reconciliation loop still can't close a gap if every surviving node is already full
Because headroom makes the reconciliation loop run faster
Because orchestrators require a fixed percentage of idle nodes by design
Headroom doesn't actually matter if the orchestrator is configured correctly
items.explanation: L2 ties headroom directly to recoverability — without it, the loop's detection and intent to fix the gap can't translate into an actual fix.
items.reference:
Why headroom matters
🈳 Spare capacity = recoverable
🈵 Fully packed = pending forever
Why: the loop can redistribute spare capacity, but it can't create capacity that isn't there.

items.prompt: According to L2, is headroom something an orchestrator provides automatically, or something that has to be planned for?
choices: Something that has to be planned for — the orchestrator only works with capacity that already exists
Something the orchestrator always provides automatically, regardless of planning
Something that only matters for clusters with a single node
Something that becomes irrelevant once self-healing is configured
items.explanation: L2 is explicit that headroom must be planned for — the orchestrator's reconciliation loop can only work with capacity that's actually available, not manufacture it.
items.reference:
Why headroom matters
🈳 Spare capacity = recoverable
🈵 Fully packed = pending forever
Why: the loop can redistribute spare capacity, but it can't create capacity that isn't there.

items.prompt: According to L3's verified Scenario A, what happened when nodeC failed after the spread scheduler placed 6 pods across 3 nodes?
choices: Both lost pods (p1, p4) were successfully rescheduled onto nodeA and nodeB, with nothing pending
All 6 pods were lost permanently
Only 1 of the 2 lost pods could be rescheduled
The reconciliation loop crashed and never recovered
items.explanation: L3 verifies that Scenario A fully recovers — both pods lost when nodeC failed were successfully rescheduled onto the surviving nodes' spare capacity.
items.reference:
Scenario A: full recovery
3 nodes, spread scheduling
nodeC fails → both pods rescheduled
Why: the earlier spread decision is what left the spare capacity recovery needed.

items.prompt: According to L3, what made Scenario A's full recovery possible?
choices: The spread scheduler's earlier decision to leave real spare capacity on every node
A special recovery mode only triggered by node failures
Having exactly 6 pods instead of some other number
The reconciliation loop retried the same node repeatedly until it worked
items.explanation: L3 attributes the successful recovery directly to the spread scheduler's initial placement, which left headroom on nodeA and nodeB before nodeC ever failed.
items.reference:
Scenario A: full recovery
3 nodes, spread scheduling
nodeC fails → both pods rescheduled
Why: the earlier spread decision is what left the spare capacity recovery needed.

items.prompt: According to L3's verified Scenario B, what happened when nodeB failed in the fully-packed 2-node cluster?
choices: Zero of the lost pods could be rescheduled — both stayed pending
Both lost pods were successfully rescheduled
One of the two lost pods was rescheduled
The scheduler automatically added a third node
items.explanation: L3 verifies that with zero headroom, the exact same reconciliation logic that fully recovered Scenario A produces zero successful placements — both pods stay pending.
items.reference:
Scenario B: no recovery
2 nodes, fully packed (0 headroom)
nodeB fails → both pods stay pending
Why: the same code, zero spare capacity — 'running correctly' isn't 'fully recovered.'

items.prompt: According to L3, was the reconciliation loop in Scenario B behaving incorrectly?
choices: No — it correctly ran and correctly reported the gap; it just had no spare capacity to close it with
Yes — a correctly implemented loop would have found capacity that didn't exist
Yes — the scheduler should have deleted pods on nodeA to make room
It's impossible to tell from L3 whether the loop behaved correctly
items.explanation: L3 is explicit: the loop is correctly running and correctly reporting the gap — the failure is a capacity-planning problem, not a bug in the reconciliation logic.
items.reference:
Scenario B: no recovery
2 nodes, fully packed (0 headroom)
nodeB fails → both pods stay pending
Why: the same code, zero spare capacity — 'running correctly' isn't 'fully recovered.'

items.prompt: Implement `scheduleSpread(nodes, pods)`, matching L3: for each pod (largest CPU/memory first), place it on the node — among those with enough remaining capacity — that has the *most* free capacity. Return `{ placements, pending, remaining }`.

tests.description: places all 6 pods from Scenario A across 3 nodes with none pending
tests.expr: (() => { const nodes = [{name:'nodeA',cpu:4,mem:8},{name:'nodeB',cpu:4,mem:8},{name:'nodeC',cpu:4,mem:8}]; const pods = [{name:'p1',cpu:1,mem:2},{name:'p2',cpu:2,mem:2},{name:'p3',cpu:1,mem:1},{name:'p4',cpu:1,mem:2},{name:'p5',cpu:2,mem:1},{name:'p6',cpu:1,mem:1}]; const r = scheduleSpread(nodes, pods); return expect(r.pending.length).toBe(0); })()

tests.description: matches L3's verified nodeC placement (p1 and p4)
tests.expr: (() => { const nodes = [{name:'nodeA',cpu:4,mem:8},{name:'nodeB',cpu:4,mem:8},{name:'nodeC',cpu:4,mem:8}]; const pods = [{name:'p1',cpu:1,mem:2},{name:'p2',cpu:2,mem:2},{name:'p3',cpu:1,mem:1},{name:'p4',cpu:1,mem:2},{name:'p5',cpu:2,mem:1},{name:'p6',cpu:1,mem:1}]; const r = scheduleSpread(nodes, pods); const onC = r.placements.filter(p => p.node === 'nodeC').map(p => p.pod).sort(); return expect(onC).toEqual(['p1', 'p4']); })()

tests.description: adds a pod to pending when no node has enough capacity
tests.expr: (() => { const nodes = [{name:'nodeA',cpu:1,mem:1}]; const pods = [{name:'huge',cpu:10,mem:10}]; const r = scheduleSpread(nodes, pods); return expect(r.pending).toEqual(['huge']); })()

items.explanation: This is the exact scheduler L3 verifies against Scenario A — picking the node with the most free capacity (rather than the first one that fits) is what spreads pods across the cluster and leaves the headroom that later makes node-failure recovery possible.
items.reference:
Spread vs. pack
📦 Pack: fills one node first
↔️ Spread: favors most free capacity
Why: spreading reduces how much one node's failure can take down.

items.prompt: Implement `schedulePack(nodes, pods)`: the opposite of `scheduleSpread` — for each pod (largest first), place it on the *first* node (in array order) with enough remaining capacity, rather than the one with the most free capacity. Return `{ placements, pending, remaining }`.

tests.description: packs nodeA fully with 2 pods before touching nodeB, on the tight 2-node scenario
tests.expr: (() => { const nodes = [{name:'nodeA',cpu:4,mem:8},{name:'nodeB',cpu:4,mem:8}]; const pods = [{name:'p1',cpu:2,mem:4},{name:'p2',cpu:2,mem:4},{name:'p3',cpu:2,mem:4},{name:'p4',cpu:2,mem:4}]; const r = schedulePack(nodes, pods); const onA = r.placements.filter(p => p.node === 'nodeA').length; return expect(onA).toBe(2); })()

tests.description: places all 4 pods with none pending when capacity allows
tests.expr: (() => { const nodes = [{name:'nodeA',cpu:4,mem:8},{name:'nodeB',cpu:4,mem:8}]; const pods = [{name:'p1',cpu:2,mem:4},{name:'p2',cpu:2,mem:4},{name:'p3',cpu:2,mem:4},{name:'p4',cpu:2,mem:4}]; const r = schedulePack(nodes, pods); return expect(r.pending.length).toBe(0); })()

tests.description: adds a pod to pending when no node has enough capacity
tests.expr: (() => { const nodes = [{name:'nodeA',cpu:1,mem:1}]; const pods = [{name:'huge',cpu:10,mem:10}]; const r = schedulePack(nodes, pods); return expect(r.pending).toEqual(['huge']); })()

items.explanation: This contrasts directly with `scheduleSpread` — using `find` instead of sorting candidates by free capacity means the first node that fits gets filled before any other node is even considered, which is the packing behavior L2 describes as risking a bigger blast radius on failure.
items.reference:
Spread vs. pack
📦 Pack: fills one node first
↔️ Spread: favors most free capacity
Why: spreading reduces how much one node's failure can take down.

items.prompt: Implement `detectGap(desiredCount, actualPods)`: given the desired replica count and an array of currently-running pod identifiers, return how many replacement pods the reconciliation loop needs to schedule (never negative).

never returns a negative gap, even with extra pods running

items.explanation: This is the comparison at the heart of L2's reconciliation flowchart — turning 'desired state' and 'actual state' into a single number that tells the loop exactly how many replacements to schedule, with no gap ever reported as negative.

Why: most cycles are boring by design — action only happens when something's actually wrong.

items.prompt: Implement `countPendingAfterNodeFailure(nodes, pods, failedNodeName)`, matching L3's Scenario A/B comparison: given `scheduleSpread` is already available, schedule the pods, simulate `failedNodeName` failing (losing whatever was placed on it), attempt to reschedule the lost pods onto the survivors, and return how many are still pending.

tests.description: matches L3's verified Scenario A: full recovery, 0 pending
tests.expr: (() => { const nodes = [{name:'nodeA',cpu:4,mem:8},{name:'nodeB',cpu:4,mem:8},{name:'nodeC',cpu:4,mem:8}]; const pods = [{name:'p1',cpu:1,mem:2},{name:'p2',cpu:2,mem:2},{name:'p3',cpu:1,mem:1},{name:'p4',cpu:1,mem:2},{name:'p5',cpu:2,mem:1},{name:'p6',cpu:1,mem:1}]; return expect(countPendingAfterNodeFailure(nodes, pods, 'nodeC')).toBe(0); })()

tests.description: matches L3's verified Scenario B: no headroom, 2 pending
tests.expr: (() => { const nodes = [{name:'nodeA',cpu:4,mem:8},{name:'nodeB',cpu:4,mem:8}]; const pods = [{name:'p1',cpu:2,mem:4},{name:'p2',cpu:2,mem:4},{name:'p3',cpu:2,mem:4},{name:'p4',cpu:2,mem:4}]; return expect(countPendingAfterNodeFailure(nodes, pods, 'nodeB')).toBe(2); })()

items.explanation: This ties the scheduler and the reconciliation loop together end to end — exactly the comparison L3 makes between Scenario A (headroom exists, full recovery) and Scenario B (zero headroom, nothing recovers), using the identical logic in both cases.
